titel: Preliminary check of a share in two hours
kurz: A review process with a fixed time budget that weeds out most candidates early and ends with a written note instead of a mere impression.

bloecke.md:
Two hours are not enough to understand a company. They are enough, however, for a reasoned decision on whether another twenty hours are worthwhile. A preliminary check is not a scaled-down valuation. Its purpose is to weed out unsuitable candidates, and to do so as early in the process as possible. If it only becomes clear after 100 minutes that the figures are unconvincing, 100 minutes are lost. If it becomes clear after twelve minutes, the evening remains for the next candidate.

This determines the order. First comes what takes little effort and often leads to the check being stopped, namely series of figures that anyone can recalculate. Last comes what is laborious and requires judgement, that is the business model, management and price. Almost everyone who later explains why the figures should be read differently in this particular case proceeds the other way round, looking first at the story told about the company and only then at the figures.

bloecke.unter: The first 70 minutes go on figures that can be recalculated, the last 50 on judgement; every stage can end with the check being stopped, which is the most common and least laborious outcome.

teile.name: Four questions: moat, management, price, risk

bloecke.md:
## Obtaining the documents (minutes 0 to 15)

The basis is the audited financial statements, not the quarterly presentation. German corporations publish those of their annual and consolidated financial statements that are subject to disclosure under Section 325 HGB (Commercial Code). For financial years from 2022, this is done via the Company Register (Unternehmensregister); older years are in the Federal Gazette (Bundesanzeiger). Both sources are free of charge and contain the notes and management report in full, unlike some glossy versions on the investor relations website. Capital-market-oriented issuers also publish an annual financial report no later than four months after the end of the financial year.

Three components of the financial statements vary in how much they yield. The notes explain the figures with disclosures on contingent liabilities, related companies, remaining maturities of debt, impairment test assumptions and audit fees. The management report under Section 289 HGB contains the forecast, opportunities and risk report and is the only mandatory forward-looking information. The cash flow statement is always a mandatory component of consolidated financial statements (Section 297(1) HGB), but in separate HGB financial statements only for capital-market-oriented companies that are not required to prepare consolidated financial statements (Section 264(1) sentence 2 HGB). It is therefore often missing for an unlisted medium-sized company, and you have to derive the cash flow yourself.

bloecke.md:
## Building the ten-year sheet (minutes 15 to 45)

Twelve rows are enough: revenue, EBIT, net profit, operating cash flow, capital expenditure, depreciation, equity, balance sheet total, financial liabilities, cash, diluted share count and dividend per share. Ten years are chosen because a decade covers a complete cycle. The years 2016 to 2025 contain the pandemic slump, the wave of inflation and the turn in the interest rate cycle. No model needs to simulate these three stress tests; they are in the figures.

The most important and at the same time least conspicuous row is the share count. Without it, you cannot tell whether growth comes from capital increases or whether jumps in profit are due to share buybacks. Each series is therefore also calculated per share. If revenue rises by 60% in ten years and the share count by 45%, revenue per share grows by around 10% and not by 60%.

Not every jump in a ten-year series has an operational cause. For financial years from 2019 onwards, IFRS 16 has put almost all leases on the balance sheet. As a result, EBITDA, balance sheet total, net debt and operating cash flow jump without a single contract having changed. Acquisitions, spin-offs, a change of reporting currency and redefined segments also shift the series. Without a marker on the sheet, you later end up comparing values that rest on different bases.

## Nine ratios in three blocks (minutes 45 to 70)

The difficulty lies less in choosing the ratios than in restricting yourself to a few. Nine ratios in three blocks are enough, and the order of the blocks determines what they say. The earnings ratios show whether there is a viable business at all. The balance sheet ratios reveal whether the company will survive the next bad year. The cash ratios check whether the results of the first two blocks are backed by cash flows.

Return on capital needs a benchmark. KPMG's cost of capital study (Kapitalkostenstudie, 2025 edition, around 300 companies, including about two thirds of the DAX 40 constituents) reports an average [[Weighted average cost of capital (WACC)|WACC]] of 8.5%, ranging by sector from 6.3% (energy and natural resources) to 9.4% (industrials, technology). The average cost of equity was 9.7%. The study, however, uses a risk-free rate of 2.5%, whereas ten-year Bunds stood at around 3.5% on 18 September 2026. The cost of capital is therefore likely to be higher by now. For the preliminary check, this means using a range of about 8% to 11% instead of a point value and checking whether the return on capital is still above it even at the upper end.

Revenue 1,200, EBIT 156, depreciation 90, interest expense 18, net profit 95 at a tax rate of 31%. Balance sheet total 1,450, equity 580, of which retained earnings 410, current assets 520, current liabilities 330, financial liabilities 390, cash 120. There are 60 million shares in issue, and the share price is €32.00.

- Net financial debt = 390 − 120 = 270. [[Enterprise value]] = 1,920 + 270 = 2,190, so EV/EBIT is 14.0.
- NOPAT = 156 × 0.69 = 108. Invested capital = 580 + 390 − 120 = 850. [[Return on invested capital (ROIC)|ROIC]] = 108 / 850 = 12.7%.
- The excess return of (12.7 − 8.5)% on 850 gives around €35 million earned each year above the cost of capital.
- Operating cash flow 165 (95 + 90 depreciation − 22 working capital + 2 other), capital expenditure 95, [[Free cash flow|free cash flow]] 70. FCF yield = 70 / 1,920 = 3.6%.

kopf: Question to ask of the series

bloecke.unter: The value of 3.06 is just above the threshold of 2.99 from which a listed industrial company is considered safe; below 1.81 lies the distress zone.

bloecke.md:
## Two scores as a quick test and their limits

The [[Altman Z-score]] condenses five balance sheet ratios into one value: Z = 1.2 X1 + 1.4 X2 + 3.3 X3 + 0.6 X4 + 1.0 X5. Here X1 is working capital, X2 retained earnings, X3 EBIT and X5 revenue, each relative to the balance sheet total. X4 is the market value of equity divided by liabilities. In the original 1968 study, the model identified around 72% of cases two years before insolvency, with 6% type II errors (healthy companies wrongly classified as at risk). The model is not designed for banks, insurers or property companies.

The share price enters the score via X4. If Example AG's share price halves without a single balance sheet figure changing, Z falls from 3.06 to 2.40 and thus into the grey zone. In this way the score adopts the market's assessment and presents it as its own result. This does not make it useless, but it is of only limited use as an early warning, because its value often falls only once the share price has already fallen.

The [[Piotroski F-score]] needs only two consecutive sets of financial statements and awards nine points: positive ROA, positive operating cash flow, higher ROA, operating cash flow above net profit, lower long-term debt ratio, higher current ratio, no new shares, higher gross margin, higher asset turnover. Eight to nine points count as strong, zero to two as weak. The values can only be compared meaningfully within one industry. In the preliminary check, the score serves less as a verdict than as a list of test questions. Each point missed shows where to look more closely in the ten-year sheet.

## Four test questions (minutes 70 to 110)

The first question concerns the economic moat. Whether there is one is shown by the figures, namely a return on capital that has been above the cost of capital for ten years and margins that do not collapse in bad years. They do not show why it exists. It must be possible to give the reason in one sentence without jargon. Typical reasons are switching costs, a brand, network effects, a cost advantage or a regulatory approval. Without this reason, there is only a statistical finding and not yet a thesis.

The second question concerns management. The most reliable indication is how the money is used. The question to answer is where the cumulative free cash flow of the last ten years has gone (into capital expenditure, acquisitions, debt repayment, dividends or buybacks) and what that has achieved. Buybacks in years of high valuation and capital increases in years of low share prices are a pattern that makes management's other statements implausible. The compensation structure shows what the company is steered towards. A bonus based on adjusted EBITDA and revenue growth leads to different decisions from one based on return on capital per share.

The third question concerns the price. No valuation is prepared here; the price is only checked for plausibility. Three comparisons are enough for this: the current multiple against the company's own ten-year range, the multiple against the industry, and the expected return against the cost of equity. For context, the US market as a whole excluding financials had an EV/EBIT of 25.7 in January 2026 (Damodaran). Only the third comparison provides a figure you can act on.

bloecke.formel: Expected return = FCF yield + growth per share ± change in valuation
bloecke.erklaerung: The formula roughly breaks down the return a share can deliver over ten years. The addition is only valid if the growth comes from investment that has already been deducted in free cash flow. Otherwise the same money is counted twice. The change in valuation is the only item that cannot be forecast. It is therefore recorded in the note as an uncertainty and not included in the calculation as a figure.
variablen: free cash flow divided by market capitalisation
sustainable growth of free cash flow per share
change in the multiple over the investment period
bloecke.beispiel: For Example AG, an FCF yield of 3.6% and growth of 4% give an expected return of 7.6%. The benchmark is the cost of equity, because the FCF yield relates to the market value of the shares. With a cost of equity of 9.7% (KPMG study) to around 11% (at today's interest rate level), this is not enough. For the calculation to work, the FCF yield would have to be between 5.7% and 7.0%. With free cash flow unchanged at €70 million, this corresponds to a share price between €20.50 (at a required return of 9.7%) and €16.70 (at 11%) instead of the current €32.00. The range is wide, but the price cannot be narrowed down more precisely in a two-hour check.

bloecke.md: The fourth question concerns risk. What is meant is not share price volatility but whatever would make the thesis worthless. Possible examples are a customer accounting for more than 10% of revenue (to be disclosed under IFRS 8), a regulatory approval, a patent, a commodity price, a lawsuit mentioned in the notes or a refinancing in the coming year. For this list, the notes are searched in a targeted way, not just skimmed. The list takes ten minutes to draw up and later determines the position size, not whether to buy or not.

bloecke.unter: Three of the outcomes lead to a no, which is what the process is for.

bloecke.md:
## Final note (minutes 110 to 120)

The note has at most four sentences. The first describes what the company does and why it earns more than its cost of capital. The second names the two or three assumptions that must continue to hold for this. The third records which observation would refute the thesis. The fourth sets the price at which to buy and the price at which not to buy any more.

The practical value lies in the archive of rejections. If it is noted why a company was rejected in March, a fresh check after a 40% share price fall in October takes only twenty minutes instead of two hours. All that then needs to be clarified is whether the reason for rejection has changed or only the price. Only in this way does the effort per company checked fall over time.

A preliminary check is successful if it quickly leads to a reasoned no. A yes is rare and comes about incidentally. It rests on a thesis, two or three assumptions and a price; conviction alone is not enough for it.

Nothing reinforces the search for confirmation as reliably as time already spent. If a problem appears after 100 minutes invested, an explanation for it will very probably be found. Two measures help against this, both taken before the check begins. First, the kill criteria are written down, for example interest cover below 2, operating cash flow below net profit in three of the last ten years, or a share count that has risen by more than 3% a year. Second, stopping the check is counted as a result and not as wasted time. The procedure also has a limit. With forged documents, no ratio calculation helps; the only option then is not to buy.

For US issuers, EDGAR replaces the Company Register. The 10-K contains the detailed risk section and management's discussion, the 20-F the same for foreign issuers, and the DEF 14A the compensation in detail. Two points easily lead to errors. The financial year often does not end in December, and revenue in foreign currencies changes the series without any operational cause. If the ten-year comparison is kept in euros, the series should also be shown alongside in the reporting currency.

Taxation does not belong in the preliminary check, but it does change the after-tax return. Capital income is subject to the flat-rate withholding tax (Abgeltungsteuer) of 25% plus solidarity surcharge (Section 32d EStG, Income Tax Act). Foreign withholding tax is credited under Section 32d(5) EStG, usually limited to the 15 percentage points permitted under the relevant double taxation agreement.

Every check uses the same twelve rows and the same nine ratios in the same order. The benefit comes less from the individual check than from the comparison. From the tenth company onwards, you can see without calculating whether a cash conversion of 1.7 is high or low for the industry in question. The first check takes four hours, the tenth two and the thirtieth one.

mitnehmen: A preliminary check is good if it quickly leads to a reasoned no; a yes is rare and comes about incidentally.
A ten-year sheet with twelve rows, also calculated per share, shows more than any single ratio from the last financial year.
Growth only creates value if the return on capital is above the cost of capital; the cost of capital should be set as a range, not as a point value.
Scores such as Altman and Piotroski are search aids and do not replace judgement; the Altman Z contains the share price and therefore reflects market opinion.
Only once the thesis, assumptions and target price have been written down has an opinion become a check.

Database of the US securities regulator SEC containing the mandatory filings of US-listed companies, including the 10-K annual report, the 20-F report of foreign issuers, the 8-K ad hoc report and the DEF 14A compensation document.
An observation defined in advance at which a check is stopped and a candidate rejected. It is noted down before the analysis of the figures begins, so that it cannot be argued away later.
The price at which a tested thesis delivers the required return. It separates the judgement on the business from the judgement on the price and is set before buying, not afterwards.
